kurals.tamil:
இரக்க இரத்தக்கார்க் காணின் கரப்பின்
அவர்பழி தம்பழி அன்று.
kurals.transliteration:
Irakka iraththakkaark kaanin karappin
avarpazhi thampazhi andru.
kurals.meaning: When you meet people it is fitting to ask, you may ask them; if they hide what they have and refuse, the blame is theirs, not yours.
kurals.elementary: Imagine you are really hungry and you politely ask a kind neighbour who has plenty of food for a little. If that neighbour pretends to have nothing, you did nothing wrong by asking. The person who hid the food is the one who acted badly.
kurals.university: The chapter on iravu (இரவு, 'asking, mendicancy') follows Nalkuravu (ch. 105, poverty) and is balanced by Iravachcham (ch. 107, dread of begging); together they permit asking only in real need and only of fitting givers. The key word irakka iraththakkaar (இரத்தக்கார், 'those of whom it is fit to ask') limits the permission: one may ask those able and willing to give. Karappin (கரப்பின், 'if they conceal') names the vice of hiding what one has, a word the chapter returns to again and again (karappu, karaththal); the commentarial line that follows Parimelazhagar, as reflected in Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan, takes the blame (pazhi) as falling wholly on the one who conceals. Pope renders it 'Theirs is the sin, not yours, if they the gift deny.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The man with food in store who, when the needy comes in miserable case begging for bread to eat, / Hardens his heart against him-even when of old he did him service-finds not one to comfort him.”
hinduism.explanation: The Vedic hymn 'Liberality' condemns the well-stocked man who hardens his heart against a hungry beggar and warns that he will himself be left without comfort.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the hymn puts the fault on the one who withholds, not on the one who asks.
hinduism.source: Rig Veda 10.117.2 (tr. Ralph T. H. Griffith)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com (hyphen as printed); close in placing blame on the refuser, though the hymn speaks of consequences rather than of blame.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Withhold not good from them to whom it is due, when it is in the power of thine hand to do it. Say not unto thy neighbour, Go, and come again, and to morrow I will give; when thou hast it by thee.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs forbids putting off a neighbour in need when one actually has what he asks for.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural's karappu, pretending to have nothing while having it, is exactly what Proverbs forbids.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (bolls.life KJV text); near one-to-one on the wrong of withholding what one has.

islam.explanation: Surah al-Ma'un ends its list of those it rebukes with people who refuse even small acts of help.
islam.tie_back: The Qur'an, like the Kural, places the fault on those who hold back help from someone who asks.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via the quran.com API; a strong thematic fit, though the verse lists the refusal among other faults rather than discussing the asker.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Beware lest you harbor the base thought, ‘The seventh year, the year of remission, is approaching,’ so that you are mean and give nothing to your needy kindred—who will cry out to God against you, and you will incur guilt.”
judaism.explanation: The Torah warns that whoever refuses a needy kinsman out of meanness incurs guilt when the poor person cries out against him.
judaism.tie_back: Deuteronomy, like the Kural, says the guilt falls on the one who refuses, not on the one who asks.
judaism.source: Deuteronomy 15:9 (The JPS Tanakh: Gender-Sensitive Edition, RJPS 2023, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified on Sefaria; the edition prints the divine name as small-caps 'GOD', rendered here as 'God'; near one-to-one on guilt falling on the withholder.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Speak the truth; yield not to anger; when asked, give even if you only have a little. By these three means can one reach the presence of the gods.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha lists giving when asked, even from little, as one of three practices that lead to the heavens.
buddhism.tie_back: Dhammapada 224 holds the person who is asked responsible for answering the request, which is where the Kural puts the duty.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; it states the giver's duty but does not speak about blame or the asker's innocence.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The hand (of the giver) is not always kindly stretched out to a monk when he is on his begging tour; but he should not think that it would be better to live as a householder.”
jainism.explanation: Among the twenty-two hardships a Jain monk must bear, Mahavira lists having to ask for everything and meeting givers whose hands are not always open.
jainism.tie_back: The Jain text admits what the Kural assumes, that some who could give will hold back, and it does not count asking as a fault in the one who asks.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; the Jain text treats a refusal as a hardship for the monk to bear, not as blame on the giver, so the fit is partial.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Your looks, my fine sir, are better than your breeding; if you were in your own house you would not spare a poor man so much as a pinch of salt, for though you are in another man's, and surrounded with abundance, you cannot find it in you to give him even a piece of bread.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Disguised as a beggar, Odysseus rebukes the suitor Antinous, who refuses him while sitting amid plenty.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The epic, like the Kural, puts the disgrace on the man who hides behind excuses and refuses, not on the beggar.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on classics.mit.edu; a vivid narrative match for blame falling on the one who withholds.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “If you have already given to anyone else, give to me also; if not, begin with me.”
philosophy.explanation: Diogenes the Cynic, who begged when he was poor, used this formula to ask for alms without apology.
philosophy.tie_back: Diogenes asked openly, as if asking a fitting person were no disgrace, which is the Kural's own position.
philosophy.source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of the Eminent Philosophers 6.49 (tr. R. D. Hicks)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Wikisource; it matches the Kural's unashamed asking but does not discuss where the blame falls.

kurals.tamil:
இன்பம் ஒருவற்கு இரத்தல் இரந்தவை
துன்பம் உறாஅ வரின்.
kurals.transliteration:
Inbam oruvarku iraththal irandhavai
thunbam uraaa varin.
kurals.meaning: Even asking can be a pleasure, if what is asked for comes without pain to either side.
kurals.elementary: If you ask a friend to share a crayon and they hand it over with a smile, asking feels nice, not embarrassing. Asking only hurts when the other person sighs or makes you feel small.
kurals.university: Valluvar makes the surprising claim that iraththal (இரத்தல், 'begging') can itself be inbam (இன்பம், 'pleasure'), on one condition: that what is begged comes thunbam uraaa (துன்பம் உறாஅ, 'without suffering'), where the lengthened uraaa is an alapedai (metrical lengthening). Commentators differ on whose suffering is meant: Mu. Varadarasanar reads it as the asker's (the gift comes without hardship), Solomon Pappaiah as the giver's reluctance, and Kalaignar as both minds, giver's and receiver's, being free of pain. The commentarial tradition following Parimelazhagar stresses that the pleasure depends on the giver's goodwill (Puliyur Kesikan: ஈவாரது நல்லுணர்வால்). Pope: 'Even to ask an alms may pleasure give, / If what you ask without annoyance you receive.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Bhagavad Gita 17.21 classes as rajasic (passionate) the charity given grudgingly, or with an eye to some return, setting it below the sattvic gift given freely out of duty.
hinduism.explanation: Krishna grades gifts by the giver's state of mind, and a grudging gift falls to the lower, passionate grade.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural's condition that the gift come 'without pain' matches the Gita's preference for gifts given without grudging.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 17.21 (paraphrase; cf. Bhagavad-gītā As It Is)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase from general knowledge of the verse, not verified verbatim this session; a strong thematic fit on the manner of giving.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
christianity.explanation: Paul asks the Corinthians to give willingly and without reluctance, because a cheerful gift is what pleases God.
christianity.tie_back: A cheerful gift is exactly what makes asking a pleasure in the Kural.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (bolls.life KJV text); close, though Paul speaks from the giver's side rather than the asker's.

islam.quote_or_event: “And as for the petitioner, do not repel [him].”
islam.explanation: God tells the Prophet not to drive away or rebuff someone who comes asking.
islam.tie_back: Not being repelled is what keeps asking free of pain, which is the Kural's condition for it being a pleasure.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via the quran.com API; it addresses the giver's manner, and the asker's pleasure is only implied.

judaism.quote_or_event: Maimonides ranks charity in eight ascending degrees, and the higher degrees are those that spare the poor person shame, for example when giver and receiver do not know each other, or when the poor person is helped to become self-supporting.
judaism.explanation: Maimonides judges a gift partly by how much it spares the recipient embarrassment.
judaism.tie_back: His concern that receiving should not hurt the poor matches the Kural's condition that the gift come without pain.
judaism.source: Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Gifts to the Poor 10:7-14 (paraphrase; tr. Eliyahu Touger available on Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased (the eight-degree ladder is well attested, but the wording was not verified this session); a strong thematic fit.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “As a bee gathers honey from the flower without injuring its color or fragrance, even so the sage goes on his alms-round in the village.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha compares the monk on his alms round to a bee that takes nectar without harming the flower.
buddhism.tie_back: Asking that harms no one is exactly the painless begging the Kural calls a pleasure.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; a near one-to-one image of asking that hurts no one.

jainism.quote_or_event: The Dasavaikalika Sutra opens (ch. 1, 'Drumapushpika') with the image of the bee that drinks from flowers without harming them, and teaches that monks should take alms from householders in the same way, accepting only what is given freely and causing no distress.
jainism.explanation: The image underlies the Jain term madhukari (bee-like) for the mendicant's alms round, in which the monk takes a little from many houses so that no family is burdened.
jainism.tie_back: The Jain rule that alms must cost the giver no hardship is the Kural's 'without pain' made into monastic discipline.
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; the bee simile in Dasavaikalika 1 is well known, but no translation was verified verbatim this session; distinct from the Buddhist Dhammapada 49 image.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Why should you want to see this stranger turned out of the house? Heaven forbid; take' something and give it him yourself; I do not grudge it; I bid you take it.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Telemachus tells Antinous to give the beggar something from the house's stores, saying he does not grudge it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: A gift offered without grudging is what makes asking pleasant, which is the Kural's point.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on classics.mit.edu (including the stray apostrophe in Butler's text); a good fit on giving without grudge, set in an ironic scene.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “He was begging of a miserly man who was slow to respond; so he said, ‘My friend, it's for food that I'm asking, not for funeral expenses.’”
philosophy.explanation: Diogenes mocks a miser whose slow, pained giving made a small request feel like a great burden.
philosophy.tie_back: The joke assumes the Kural's point: asking turns sour when the gift comes with pain.
philosophy.source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of the Eminent Philosophers 6.56 (tr. R. D. Hicks)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Wikisource (inner quotation marks normalised); it shows the opposite case only, so the match is indirect.

kurals.tamil:
கரப்பிலா நெஞ்சின் கடனறிவார் முன்நின்று
இரப்புமோ ரேஎர் உடைத்து.
kurals.transliteration:
Karappilaa nenjin kadanarivaar munnindru
irappumor eer udaiththu.
kurals.meaning: To stand before people whose hearts hide nothing and who know their duty, and ask of them, even that has a certain grace.
kurals.elementary: Asking your grandmother, who loves to share, for a slice of cake doesn't feel bad at all. It can even feel nice, because she is happy you asked.
kurals.university: Karappilaa nenju (கரப்பிலா நெஞ்சு, 'a heart without concealment') and kadan arivaar (கடனறிவார், 'those who know their duty') describe the ideal giver. Kadan is read as duty (Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah: 'this is my duty'), while Puliyur Kesikan glosses the givers as people who understand honour (மானம் அறிபவர்). The striking word is eer (ஏஎர், with alapedai lengthening, 'beauty, grace'): standing before such givers, even begging has beauty. The commentarial tradition following Parimelazhagar reads the -um in irappum ('even begging') as conceding that begging is normally without grace. Pope: 'To stand as suppliants affords especial grace.' Texts on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net agree, both printing the sandhi form இரப்புமோ ரேஎர்.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Charity given out of duty, without expectation of return, at the proper time and place, and to a worthy person is considered to be in the mode of goodness.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna calls sattvic, the highest kind, the gift given simply because it ought to be given (dātavyam iti), with no thought of return.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural's kadan arivaar, givers who know their duty, are the Gita's sattvic givers.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 17.20 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on vedabase.io; close on giving as duty, though the Gita does not speak of the asker's grace.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Give to him that asketh thee, and from him that would borrow of thee turn not thou away.”
christianity.explanation: In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus tells his followers simply to give to whoever asks.
christianity.tie_back: Givers who never turn away a request are the open-hearted givers before whom the Kural says even asking has grace.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (bolls.life KJV text); a strong fit on the giver's open heart, and the asker's dignity is implied.

islam.quote_or_event: “And from their properties was [given] the right of the [needy] petitioner and the deprived.”
islam.explanation: Describing the righteous, the Qur'an says that the asker and the deprived had a right (haqq) in their wealth.
islam.tie_back: If the asker has a right to a share, then asking such people is not shameful, which is close to the Kural's 'grace'.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via the quran.com API; givers who treat giving as a debt owed match kadan arivaar closely.

judaism.quote_or_event: “do not harden your heart and shut your hand against your needy kindred. Rather, you must open your hand and lend whatever is sufficient to meet the need.”
judaism.explanation: The Torah commands an open hand and an unhardened heart toward a needy kinsman, and lending enough to meet the need.
judaism.tie_back: The open hand and unhardened heart are the Kural's karappilaa nenju, the heart that hides nothing.
judaism.source: Deuteronomy 15:7-8 (The JPS Tanakh: Gender-Sensitive Edition, RJPS 2023, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria (opening clause omitted); a strong fit on the open-hearted giver, though silent on the asker's grace.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “I am a brahman, responsive to requests, open-handed, bearing my last body, an unsurpassed doctor & surgeon.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha describes himself as one who answers requests with an open hand, and then says that the gift of Dhamma is the highest gift.
buddhism.tie_back: 'Responsive to requests, open-handed' describes the kind of giver before whom, the Kural says, asking has grace.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; the self-description fits the ideal giver, though the passage goes on to the gift of Dhamma, not material alms.

jainism.quote_or_event: Atithi-samvibhaga, 'sharing with the guest', is one of the vows of the Jain householder: a duty to share pure food and requisites with mendicants who arrive unannounced.
jainism.explanation: Jain householders treat sharing with an arriving ascetic as a vow, part of their duty, rather than as an optional favour.
jainism.tie_back: A giver for whom sharing is a vow is the Kural's kadan arivaar, someone who knows giving as a duty.
jainism.source: Tattvartha Sutra 7 (list of householder vows, incl. atithi-samvibhaga; verse numbering differs between Svetambara and Digambara recensions) (paraphrase)
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; the vow is standard Jain doctrine but no translation was verified verbatim this session; the fit is to the giver's duty, not to the asker's grace.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Take this to the stranger, and tell him to go the round of the suitors, and beg from them; a beggar must not be shamefaced.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Telemachus sends the disguised Odysseus a whole loaf and tells him that a beggar need not be ashamed to ask.
greek_mythology.tie_back: In a house where the host gives freely, asking carries no shame, which is the Kural's point.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on classics.mit.edu; it fits the dignity of asking from a generous host, although the suitors he is sent to are not such givers.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle says the liberal (generous) person gives for the sake of what is noble and gives rightly: to the right people, in the right amounts, at the right time, and with pleasure rather than pain.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, liberality is a settled disposition to give well, not an occasional act.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural's ideal giver, open-hearted and knowing his duty, is close to Aristotle's liberal man.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 4.1 (tr. W. D. Ross) (paraphrase)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase from the Ross translation, not verified verbatim this session; the fit is to the giver's disposition.

kurals.tamil:
இரத்தலும் ஈதலே போலும் கரத்தல்
கனவிலும் தேற்றாதார் மாட்டு.
kurals.transliteration:
Iraththalum eedhale polum karaththal
kanavilum thetraadhaar maattu.
kurals.meaning: Asking of people who would never think of withholding, even in a dream, is as honourable as giving.
kurals.elementary: Some people love sharing so much that when you ask them, it's like you're doing them a favour. With friends like that, asking feels almost as good as giving.
kurals.university: The line iraththalum eedhale polum (இரத்தலும் ஈதலே போலும், 'begging too is just like giving') is one of the boldest claims in the Kural, and the emphatic ē in eedhale strengthens the equation. Its condition is that the giver karaththal kanavilum thetraadhaar (கரத்தல் கனவிலும் தேற்றாதார், 'does not know concealment even in a dream'). Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar all read it as conferring the same dignity (சிறப்பு, பெருமை) on such asking as on giving. The commentarial tradition following Parimelazhagar explains the equation by the giver's joy: asking such a person gives him the chance to give. Pope: 'To beg of such ... is in fact the same as giving.' The texts on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net agree.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Vamana episode, Vishnu takes the form of a dwarf brahmin and asks King Bali for three paces of land. Bali gives without holding back, even after his preceptor warns him, and his giving earns him lasting glory and divine favour.
hinduism.explanation: When God himself becomes the asker, the request turns into an honour and a blessing for the one who gives.
hinduism.tie_back: The story makes the Kural's paradox literal: asking a giver who never withholds is a gift to that giver.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known episode; it fits the asking-as-gift idea, but the asker is divine and the request is a test, so the match is partial.

christianity.quote_or_event: The prophet Elijah asks a starving widow of Zarephath for water and a little bread, made from her last flour and oil. She gives, and her barrel of meal and cruse of oil do not run out for the rest of the famine.
christianity.explanation: The prophet's request, which looked like a burden on the widow, turned out to be a blessing for her.
christianity.tie_back: Asking a giver who does not hold back becomes, as the Kural says, like giving.
christianity._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the narrative; a good illustration of asking that turns into a gift to the giver, but the text makes no general claim.

islam.quote_or_event: “[Saying], "We feed you only for the face [i.e., approval] of Allāh. We wish not from you reward or gratitude."”
islam.explanation: The righteous feed the needy, the orphan and the captive, and tell them that they want no reward or even thanks.
islam.tie_back: When a giver wants nothing back, the receiver owes nothing and is not lowered, so asking such a person costs no honour.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via the quran.com API; it describes the giver who never withholds, while the equation of asking with giving is implied.

judaism.quote_or_event: “More than what the homeowner does for the poor person, the poor person does for the homeowner”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Yehoshua reads Ruth's words about Boaz, 'for whom I acted today', as showing that by accepting his bread she did him a greater favour, giving him the merit of charity.
judaism.tie_back: The midrash says almost exactly what the Kural says: the one who receives also gives.
judaism.source: Vayikra Rabbah 34:8 (The Sefaria Midrash Rabbah, 2022, tr. Joshua Schreier)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; a near one-to-one match for 'asking is just like giving'.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Monks, brahmans & householders are very helpful to you, as they provide you with the requisites of robes, alms food, lodgings, & medical requisites for the sick. And you, monks, are very helpful to brahmans & householders, as you teach them the Dhamma”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha describes a two-way exchange: lay people give material support, and the monks who receive it give the Dhamma in return.
buddhism.tie_back: The almsman who asks is also a giver, which is the Kural's equation of asking with giving.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org (excerpt); close, though the monk's return gift is teaching rather than the giver's merit.

jainism.quote_or_event: The Tattvartha Sutra defines dana (giving) as parting with one's own things for anugraha, the benefit of both oneself and the other, and teaches that its fruit depends on the manner, the thing given, the giver and the recipient.
jainism.explanation: In Jain doctrine a gift benefits the giver as much as the receiver, through the merit and the loosening of attachment it brings.
jainism.tie_back: If giving benefits both sides equally, then asking and giving share in the same good, which is the Kural's claim.
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the dana sutras; the 'mutual benefit' definition is standard, but no translation was verified verbatim this session.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “I too was a rich man once, and had a fine house of my own; in those days I gave to many a tramp such as I now am, no matter who he might be nor what he wanted.”
greek_mythology.explanation: The disguised Odysseus tells Antinous that he was once a rich giver to every tramp, and now stands asking himself.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Asker and giver are the same man at different times, which hints at the Kural's equation of the two.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on classics.mit.edu; it brings asking and giving together through one life rather than stating their equality.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Being asked why people give to beggars but not to philosophers, he said, ‘Because they think they may one day be lame or blind, but never expect that they will turn to philosophy.’”
philosophy.explanation: Diogenes says that people give to beggars because they can picture themselves in the beggar's place.
philosophy.tie_back: His answer touches the Kural's insight that giver and asker are not so far apart.
philosophy.source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of the Eminent Philosophers 6.56 (tr. R. D. Hicks)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Wikisource (inner quotation marks normalised); next-best only, since the point is the giver's motive, not the dignity of asking.

kurals.tamil:
கரப்பிலார் வையகத்து உண்மையால் கண்ணின்று
இரப்பவர் மேற்கொள் வது.
kurals.transliteration:
Karappilaar vaiyagaththu unmaiyaal kannindru
irappavar merkol vadhu.
kurals.meaning: It is only because there are people in the world who never hold back that some take up asking, standing before others' eyes.
kurals.elementary: People bring their empty buckets to a well because they know the well has water. In the same way, people in need ask because they know there are kind people who will share.
kurals.university: The kural explains why anyone begs at all: because karappilaar (கரப்பிலார், 'those without concealment') exist in the world (vaiyagaththu unmaiyaal). Kan nindru (கண்ணின்று, 'standing before the eyes') is read in two ways: Mu. Varadarasanar takes it as standing in front of a giver, while Solomon Pappaiah reads it as asking with the eyes rather than with words, the silent request of the proud poor. Puliyur Kesikan adds that such people beg only to preserve life. The sense of merkolvadhu (மேற்கொள்வது, 'taking up' a practice) suggests begging chosen reluctantly because generous givers are known to exist. The texts on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net agree (மேற்கொள் வது with a space in both).

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Bounteous is he who gives unto the beggar who comes to him in want of food and feeble.”
hinduism.explanation: The Vedic hymn names as truly bountiful the man who gives to a feeble beggar who comes to him.
hinduism.tie_back: The beggar comes to him because such a giver exists, which is the logic of the Kural.
hinduism.source: Rig Veda 10.117.3 (tr. Ralph T. H. Griffith)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; it describes the giver the beggar approaches, while the Kural's explanation of why people beg is only implied.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And a certain man lame from his mother's womb was carried, whom they laid daily at the gate of the temple which is called Beautiful, to ask alms of them that entered into the temple”
christianity.explanation: A lame man is carried every day to the temple gate, where worshippers pass and might give.
christianity.tie_back: He is placed where givers are known to pass, which illustrates the Kural's point that asking exists because givers exist.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (bolls.life KJV text); a narrative illustration rather than a teaching.

islam.quote_or_event: “An ignorant [person] would think them self-sufficient because of their restraint, but you will know them by their [characteristic] sign. They do not ask people persistently [or at all].”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an describes poor people too dignified to ask, who must be recognised by their look rather than by any words.
islam.tie_back: This is Pappaiah's reading of kan nindru: the poor who ask with their eyes, trusting that a discerning giver will see.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via the quran.com API (excerpt); a strong match for the silent, eye-level asking in one reading of the kural.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Let thy house be wide open, and let the poor be members of thy household.”
judaism.explanation: Yose ben Yochanan teaches that a home should stand open so that the poor come in as if they belonged.
judaism.tie_back: A house whose door is always open is why the needy come to it, which is the Kural's reasoning.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 1:5 (Mishnah Yomit, tr. Dr. Joshua Kulp, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; strong on the open-handed house that draws the needy.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Alms food is next to nothing, both easy to gain & blameless.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha counts alms food among the requisites that are easy to get, so a monk can rely on it.
buddhism.tie_back: Alms are 'easy to gain' only because there are generous givers, which the Kural gives as the reason people take up asking.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; it assumes rather than states that givers make the mendicant life possible.

jainism.quote_or_event: After Rishabhanatha renounced the world, people did not know how to give a mendicant proper alms. They offered jewels, horses and even daughters, and he went without food for about a year until Prince Shreyamsa recognised the right way and offered him sugarcane juice, the event remembered on Akshaya Tritiya.
jainism.explanation: The Jain tradition holds that the mendicant's alms round could only work once there were householders who knew how to give.
jainism.tie_back: The story dramatises the Kural's point: asking depends on the existence of givers who know how to give.
jainism.source: Hemacandra, Trishashtishalakapurushacharitra, Book 1 (life of Rishabha) (tr. Helen M. Johnson) (paraphrase)
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a widely told Jain narrative; not verified verbatim this session; a good fit on mendicancy depending on knowing givers.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “a beggar can always do better in town than country, for any one who likes can give him something.”
greek_mythology.explanation: The disguised Odysseus says a beggar should go where there are many people able to give.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Beggars go where givers are, which is the Kural's explanation of why people take up asking.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on classics.mit.edu; a close practical version of the Kural's reasoning.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “He was known as the ‘Door-opener’ – the caller to whom all doors fly open – from his habit of entering every house and admonishing those within.”
philosophy.explanation: The Cynic Crates lived without property and was welcome in every Athenian house.
philosophy.tie_back: He could live by asking only because doors opened to him, which is the Kural's point that asking exists because open-handed people exist.
philosophy.source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of the Eminent Philosophers 6.86 (tr. R. D. Hicks)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Wikisource (inner quotation marks normalised); a reasonable but partial fit, since Crates gave advice rather than simply asking.

kurals.tamil:
கரப்பிடும்பை யில்லாரைக் காணின் நிரப்பிடும்பை
எல்லாம் ஒருங்கு கெடும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Karappidumbai yillaaraik kaanin nirappidumbai
ellaam orungu kedum.
kurals.meaning: At the mere sight of those free from the affliction of withholding, all the afflictions of want vanish at once.
kurals.elementary: When a hungry child sees a kind lunch lady who always shares, the worry disappears right away. Just seeing someone generous makes the scary feeling go.
kurals.university: The kural plays on two compounds built on idumbai (இடும்பை, 'affliction'): karappidumbai, the affliction (or 'disease', in Pappaiah's gloss நோய்) of concealment that belongs to the miser, and nirappidumbai, the affliction of want that belongs to the poor. The miser's karappu is thus treated as a sickness of its own, the counterpart of the beggar's poverty. Kaanin (காணின், 'if one but sees') shows that the mere sight of such a giver ends ellaam orungu (எல்லாம் ஒருங்கு, 'all together') the beggar's distress. Puliyur Kesikan adds that this holds for one who begs without losing self-respect (மானம் விடாமல்), and Kalaignar calls concealment an இழிநிலை (base state). The texts on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net agree, both printing the sandhi form யில்லாரைக்.

hinduism.quote_or_event: King Rantideva, after fasting for forty-eight days, gives away his food and water in turn to a brahmin, a shudra, a man with dogs and finally an outcaste, praying only to take on the sufferings of all beings so that they may be free of pain.
hinduism.explanation: Rantideva's giving is so complete that every hungry person who comes to him leaves relieved.
hinduism.tie_back: A giver with no trace of withholding ends the misery of those who come to him, as the Kural says.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known episode; not re-verified verbatim this session; good on the giver without withholding, though the Kural stresses the effect of merely seeing him.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Then Peter said, Silver and gold have I none; but such as I have give I thee: In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth rise up and walk.”
christianity.explanation: The lame beggar asks Peter for alms; Peter gives what he has, healing, and the man leaps up praising God.
christianity.tie_back: One meeting with an unstinting giver ends all of the beggar's affliction, the Kural's ellaam orungu kedum.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (bolls.life KJV text); striking because the beggar's whole condition ends at once, though the gift is miraculous rather than material.

islam.quote_or_event: The Prophet taught that whoever relieves a believer of one of the hardships of this world, God will relieve him of one of the hardships of the Day of Resurrection, and that God helps a servant as long as the servant helps his brother.
islam.explanation: The hadith treats removing another's distress as one of the most rewarded acts.
islam.tie_back: It stresses, as the Kural does, that a generous person can lift a needy person's affliction.
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; not re-verified verbatim this session; the Kural's specific idea that the giver's mere sight ends want is absent.

judaism.quote_or_event: “For I saved the pauper who cried out, / The orphan who had no helper. / I received the blessing of the lost; / I gladdened the heart of the widow.”
judaism.explanation: Job remembers his days of prosperity, when the poor who cried to him were rescued and the widow's heart was made glad.
judaism.tie_back: Job is the giver without the 'disease of withholding' whose presence ended the distress of those who turned to him.
judaism.source: Job 29:12-13 (The JPS Tanakh: Gender-Sensitive Edition, RJPS 2023, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; good on the giver ending distress, though not on 'mere sight'.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The householder Sudatta was so constant in feeding the destitute that he became known as Anathapindika, 'feeder of the unprotected', and the tradition counts him the foremost lay donor among the Buddha's followers.
buddhism.explanation: His very name came to mean relief for the helpless who came to him.
buddhism.tie_back: A giver known never to hold back, whose name alone promises relief, fits the Kural's image well.
buddhism.source: Pali tradition on Anathapindika (e.g., SN 10.8; AN 1 'foremost' lists) (paraphrase)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a composite tradition; not verified verbatim this session; illustrative rather than doctrinal.

jainism.quote_or_event: Jain householder ethics lists four kinds of gift: ahara-dana (food), aushadha-dana (medicine), abhaya-dana (protection from fear) and jnana-dana (knowledge), which together aim to remove every kind of want.
jainism.explanation: Taken together, the four gifts address hunger, sickness, fear and ignorance, the whole range of a needy person's distress.
jainism.tie_back: The fourfold gift is a Jain picture of how a giver free of withholding can end all of a seeker's afflictions at once.
jainism.source: V. A. Sangave, Jaina ethics (jainworld.com), on the four kinds of dana (paraphrase)
jainism._accuracy_note: Next-best only: the fourfold dana is standard Jain teaching but was not verified verbatim this session, and the Kural's focus on the giver's mere sight is missing.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “the other suitors all gave him something, and filled his wallet with bread and meat”
greek_mythology.explanation: Most of the suitors give to the disguised Odysseus and fill his wallet.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Among those who did not withhold, the beggar's want was met at once, a partial picture of the Kural's claim.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on classics.mit.edu; next-best only, since the suitors are not models of generosity and the Kural's point about the giver's sight is absent.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca urges that a benefit be given promptly and without hesitation, since a gift that is long delayed and grudgingly given loses much of its value to the one who receives it.
philosophy.explanation: For Seneca, the giver's readiness is itself part of the benefit.
philosophy.tie_back: A giver with no impulse to hold back relieves need at once, which is the effect the Kural describes.
philosophy.source: Seneca, On Benefits, Book II (tr. Aubrey Stewart) (paraphrase)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Next-best paraphrase; not verified verbatim this session; it addresses promptness rather than the relief brought by the giver's presence.

kurals.tamil:
இகழ்ந்தெள்ளாது ஈவாரைக் காணின் மகிழ்ந்துள்ளம்
உள்ளுள் உவப்பது உடைத்து.
kurals.transliteration:
Igazhndhellaadhu eevaaraik kaanin magizhndhullam
ullul uvappadhu udaiththu.
kurals.meaning: When the asker meets givers who give without scorn or ridicule, his heart rejoices deep within.
kurals.elementary: If you ask for help and the person helps you with a kind smile instead of laughing at you, you feel warm and happy inside. How we give matters as much as what we give.
kurals.university: Igazhndhu ellaadhu (இகழ்ந்து எள்ளாது, 'without despising, without mocking') names the two insults a giver can add to a gift, contempt and derision; Pappaiah glosses them as அவமதிக்காமல், இழிவாகப் பேசாமல். The response is doubled for emphasis: magizhndhu (மகிழ்ந்து, 'rejoicing') and ullul uvappadhu (உள்ளுள் உவப்பது, 'delighting within the innermost heart'). The commentarial tradition following Parimelazhagar places the joy in the asker, and the next chapter, Iravachcham, will show the opposite case, where contempt makes asking unbearable. Pope: 'The minds of askers, through and through, will thrill with joy.' The texts on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net agree.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “And charity performed at an impure place, at an improper time, to unworthy persons, or without proper attention and respect is said to be in the mode of ignorance.”
hinduism.explanation: The Gita places at the lowest grade the gift given without respect (asat-kṛtam) and with disdain (avajñātam).
hinduism.tie_back: The Gita's avajñātam, contempt, is exactly the scorn (igazhchi, ellal) that the Kural says spoils a gift.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 17.22 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on vedabase.io; near one-to-one on contemptuous giving, though seen from the giver's side.

christianity.quote_or_event: “If any of you lack wisdom, let him ask of God, that giveth to all men liberally, and upbraideth not; and it shall be given him.”
christianity.explanation: James invites believers to ask God freely, because God gives generously and does not reproach the one who asks.
christianity.tie_back: 'Giveth liberally, and upbraideth not' is almost word for word the Kural's 'gives without scorn or ridicule'.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on kingjamesbibleonline.org; very close wording, with God as the model giver.

islam.quote_or_event: “Kind speech and forgiveness are better than charity followed by injury. And Allāh is Free of need and Forbearing.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an ranks a kind word above a gift that is followed by hurt or humiliation.
islam.tie_back: The Kural's joy at a gift given without scorn is the other side of the Qur'an's warning against gifts that injure.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via the quran.com API; a close match on the manner of giving.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Whenever a person gives charity to a poor person with an unpleasant countenance and with his face buried in the earth, he loses and destroys his merit even if he gives him 1000 gold pieces. Instead, he should give him with a pleasant countenance and with happiness, commiserating with him about his troubles”
judaism.explanation: Maimonides rules that a gift given with a sour face loses all merit, while a gift given cheerfully and with sympathy is the proper way.
judaism.tie_back: This states the Kural's lesson as law: the manner of a gift decides whether the poor person's heart is gladdened.
judaism.source: Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Gifts to the Poor 10:4 (tr. Eliyahu Touger, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria (footnote marker removed); near one-to-one.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Sappurisadana Sutta the Buddha lists the gifts of a person of integrity: given with conviction, attentively and with respect, at the right time, with an empathetic heart, and without harming oneself or others, and each brings its own good result.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that a gift given respectfully and with empathy differs in kind from one carelessly thrown.
buddhism.tie_back: Giving with respect and empathy is what produces the asker's inner joy in the Kural.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the sutta's list; not verified verbatim this session; a strong thematic fit.

jainism.quote_or_event: In the Uttaradhyayana's twelfth lecture, the outcaste-born monk Harikesa comes begging to a Brahmin sacrifice and is mocked and beaten. A yaksha who serves him intervenes, and the Brahmins finally honour him and give him alms.
jainism.explanation: The story condemns those who insult a mendicant and shows that a gift offered with respect is what honours both sides.
jainism.tie_back: It is a negative example of the Kural's lesson: scorn spoils the giving, and respect brings joy.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Lecture 12 (Harikesa) (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45) (paraphrase)
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the lecture's narrative; not verified verbatim this session; a reasonable fit by contrast.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “With these words he threw a footstool at him, and hit him on the right shoulder-blade near the top of his back.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Antinous answers the disguised Odysseus's request by throwing a footstool at him, and even the other suitors are shocked.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the opposite of the giver the Kural praises, and it shows why a gift without scorn gladdens the heart.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on classics.mit.edu; a vivid contrast case.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca reports that Fabius Verrucosus called a favour granted harshly by an unfeeling man 'bread full of stones': welcome to a hungry man, but painful to swallow.
philosophy.explanation: Seneca holds that the manner of giving can spoil the benefit itself.
philosophy.tie_back: A gift given with scorn is the stony bread the Kural's asker cannot enjoy, while one given kindly makes the heart rejoice.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; the 'bread full of stones' saying is in De Beneficiis 2.7, but the wording was not verified this session.

kurals.tamil:
இரப்பாரை இல்லாயின் ஈர்ங்கண்மா ஞாலம்
மரப்பாவை சென்றுவந் தற்று.
kurals.transliteration:
Irappaarai illaayin eerngkanmaa nyaalam
marappaavai sendruvan thatru.
kurals.meaning: If there were no askers, the comings and goings of this cool, wide world would be no more than wooden puppets moving to and fro.
kurals.elementary: Imagine a toy theatre where wooden puppets bounce around on strings. They move, but they don't really care about anything. Valluvar says that if no one ever needed help, people would be like those puppets, busy but with no kindness to show.
kurals.university: Eerngkanmaa nyaalam (ஈர்ங்கண்மா ஞாலம், 'the cool, wide, great earth') and marappaavai (மரப்பாவை, 'wooden doll') give the image: Mu. Varadarasanar explains it as a wooden puppet moved by strings, so that human activity without askers would be mechanical motion without inner meaning. The commentarial tradition following Parimelazhagar takes the point to be that giving is what gives life its moral content, and giving needs askers. Kalaignar reads the couplet differently, making those who keep the poor at a distance no different from operated puppets. Pope: 'The mighty earth ... Will be a stage where wooden puppets come and go.' The texts on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net agree (சென்றுவந் தற்று in both).

hinduism.quote_or_event: “He feeds no trusty friend, no man to love him. All guilt is he who eats with no partaker.”
hinduism.explanation: The Vedic hymn says that someone who eats without sharing is 'all guilt', his life empty of bonds of love.
hinduism.tie_back: A life with no one to share with has lost its point, which comes close to the Kural's world of puppets.
hinduism.source: Rig Veda 10.117.6 (tr. Ralph T. H. Griffith)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; next-best only, since the hymn condemns the non-sharer rather than saying that askers give the world meaning.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me.”
christianity.explanation: In the judgment scene, Christ says that what is done for the hungry, the stranger and the poor is done for him.
christianity.tie_back: Without the needy there would be no meeting with Christ through them, an echo of the Kural's claim that askers give the world its meaning.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (bolls.life KJV text); a reasonable but partial fit, since the Kural's point is about the meaning of human action.

islam.quote_or_event: “The example of those who spend their wealth in the way of Allāh is like a seed [of grain] which grows seven spikes; in each spike is a hundred grains.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an compares charity to a seed that multiplies into hundreds of grains.
islam.tie_back: Giving is what makes wealth grow and bear fruit, and there is no giving without someone to receive.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via the quran.com API (excerpt); next-best only, since the verse does not speak of a world without askers.

judaism.quote_or_event: “the world stands upon three things: the Torah, the Temple service, and the practice of acts of piety.”
judaism.explanation: Shimon the Righteous names acts of kindness (gemilut chasadim) as one of the three pillars that hold up the world.
judaism.tie_back: If kindness is a pillar of the world, a world with no one to receive it would lose something essential, close to the Kural's image.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 1:2 (Mishnah Yomit, tr. Dr. Joshua Kulp, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; a reasonable thematic fit, though the mishnah does not mention askers.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the recollection of the Sangha recited in the Dhajagga Sutta, the community of noble disciples is called worthy of gifts and of hospitality and 'an unsurpassed field of merit for the world'.
buddhism.explanation: Buddhist teaching treats the alms-receiving community as the 'field' in which the world's giving bears fruit.
buddhism.tie_back: Without such a field the world's generosity would have nowhere to take root, near the Kural's claim that askers give the world meaning.
buddhism.source: Dhajagga Sutta, SN 11.3 (recollection of the Sangha) (paraphrase)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; the formula is standard but was not re-verified verbatim this session; the 'field of merit' concerns monks, not ordinary beggars.

jainism.quote_or_event: Jain teaching on householder conduct (vaiyavrittya and gifts to ascetics) describes householders and mendicants as depending on each other: monks rely on pure alms freely given, and householders gain merit and spiritual progress by giving.
jainism.explanation: In Jain practice, lay giving finds its fullest meaning in supporting the mendicant order.
jainism.tie_back: A world with no one to give to would empty this exchange, roughly what the Kural pictures.
jainism.source: Samantabhadra, Ratnakaranda Shravakachara (section on vaiyavrittya / gifts) (paraphrase)
jainism._accuracy_note: Next-best paraphrase, not verified verbatim this session; it concerns mendicant monks, not the poor in general.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “we know the gods go about disguised in all sorts of ways as people from foreign countries, and travel about the world to see who do amiss and who righteously.”
greek_mythology.explanation: A suitor warns Antinous that a beggar may be a god in disguise, testing who behaves rightly.
greek_mythology.tie_back: In the Greek view the beggar at the door is how a person's character is shown, a sense close to the Kural's claim that askers give human life its meaning.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on classics.mit.edu; a reasonable fit, since the beggar is the occasion for virtue or vice.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca opens On Benefits by treating the giving and receiving of benefits as the practice that, more than any other, holds human society together.
philosophy.explanation: For Seneca, benefits are a social bond, not a private transaction.
philosophy.tie_back: Without people in need of benefits that bond would vanish, like the Kural's world of puppets.
philosophy.source: Seneca, On Benefits, Book I (tr. Aubrey Stewart) (paraphrase)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; not verified verbatim this session; a reasonable thematic fit.

kurals.tamil:
ஈவார்கண் என்னுண்டாம் தோற்றம் இரந்துகோள்
மேவார் இலாஅக் கடை.
kurals.transliteration:
Eevaarkan ennundaam thotram irandhukol
mevaar ilaaak kadai.
kurals.meaning: What glory could givers have if there were no one who wished to ask and receive?
kurals.elementary: A goalkeeper can only be a hero if someone kicks the ball. In the same way, a generous person can only shine if someone needs their help.
kurals.university: Thotram (தோற்றம், 'appearance, eminence') is glossed as pugazh (புகழ், 'fame') by Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar. Irandhu kol mevaar (இரந்துகோள் மேவார், 'those who wish to take by asking') are the counterpart without whom the giver's eminence cannot exist; ilaaak kadai has the alapedai lengthening ilaaa. Read with 1058, the couplet pair makes askers necessary to the moral economy of giving, a theme going back to Ch. 23 (Eegai) and Ch. 24 (Pugazh), where fame is linked to giving. Pope: 'What glory will there be to men of generous soul, / When none are found to love the askers' role?' The texts on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net agree.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Karna, famed as the great giver, never refused anyone who came asking. When Indra came disguised as a brahmin and asked for his natural armour and earrings, Karna cut them from his body and gave them, though it cost him his protection, and that gift sealed his fame.
hinduism.explanation: Karna's lasting glory as dana-vira, the hero of giving, rests on the askers he never turned away.
hinduism.tie_back: Without Indra's request there would be no story of Karna's supreme gift, as the Kural says: a giver's glory needs askers.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Kundala-harana sub-parva (tr. K. M. Ganguli) (paraphrase)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known episode; not verified verbatim this session; a strong narrative fit.

christianity.quote_or_event: “It is more blessed to give than to receive.”
christianity.explanation: Paul quotes a saying of Jesus that giving brings a greater blessing than receiving.
christianity.tie_back: If giving is the greater blessing, then receivers make that blessing possible, which is the Kural's point.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (bolls.life KJV text); the Kural draws the inference about receivers that the verse leaves implicit.

islam.quote_or_event: “O people! Give in charity as a time will come upon you when a person will wander about with his object of charity and will not find anybody to accept it”
islam.explanation: The Prophet urges people to give now, warning of a time when there will be no one left to accept charity.
islam.tie_back: He pictures exactly the world the Kural imagines, where givers can find no askers and lose their chance of merit.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sunnah.com (excerpt); a near one-to-one picture of givers with no one to receive.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Rabbi Akiva said to him: He commands us to sustain the poor, so that through them and the charity we give them we will be saved from the judgment of Gehenna.”
judaism.explanation: Answering why God does not feed the poor himself, Rabbi Akiva says the poor exist so that givers may earn merit through them.
judaism.tie_back: The poor are the means of the givers' merit, the Kural's point that askers make givers great.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Bava Batra 10a (William Davidson Edition, Koren-Steinsaltz, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified on Sefaria with the bold-face markup removed; a close fit, with merit in place of fame.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Prince Vessantara, in the Bodhisattva's last human birth before Gotama, gives away everything he is asked for, from the kingdom's white elephant to his own children, and his perfection of generosity (dana-parami) becomes legendary because of those who came asking.
buddhism.explanation: Vessantara's fame as the perfect giver rests on a series of supplicants.
buddhism.tie_back: Without askers, Vessantara's perfection of giving could not have been shown, which is the Kural's claim.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a widely known Jataka; not verified verbatim this session; a strong narrative fit.

jainism.quote_or_event: Chandana (Chandanbala), a princess sold into servitude and kept in chains, offered boiled lentils to Mahavira at the end of his long fast, fulfilling the strict conditions of his abhigraha vow; her gift made her famous, and she later became head of his order of nuns.
jainism.explanation: In Jain memory Chandana's glory comes from having been the one able to give to the great ascetic.
jainism.tie_back: Her fame as a giver depended on the asker, Mahavira, which is the Kural's point.
jainism.source: Hemacandra, Trishashtishalakapurushacharitra, Book 10 (life of Mahavira) (tr. Helen M. Johnson) (paraphrase)
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known Jain narrative; not verified verbatim this session; reasonable fit.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “you seem to be a chief, foremost among them all; therefore you should be the better giver, and I will tell far and wide of your bounty.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus, disguised as a beggar, offers Antinous fame in return for a gift: the beggar will spread the giver's name.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The beggar holds the key to the giver's renown, which is the Kural's idea in story form.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on classics.mit.edu; a near one-to-one link between the asker and the giver's fame.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle notes that liberal people are among the most loved of virtuous characters because they are useful to others, and that this depends on their giving.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, the honour of the liberal man rests on his giving to others.
philosophy.tie_back: Since that honour depends on giving, it depends on recipients, which matches the Kural's question.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 4.1 (tr. W. D. Ross) (paraphrase)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase from the Ross translation, not verified verbatim this session; a reasonable fit.

kurals.tamil:
இரப்பான் வெகுளாமை வேண்டும் நிரப்பிடும்பை
தானேயும் சாலும் கரி.
kurals.transliteration:
Irappaan vegulaamai vendum nirappidumbai
thaaneyum saalum kari.
kurals.meaning: One who asks must not grow angry when refused; his own distress of want is proof enough of how things stand.
kurals.elementary: If you ask a friend to share and they say no, don't get mad. You know how it feels not to have enough, so maybe they don't have enough either, or maybe it just wasn't the right time.
kurals.university: Vegulaamai (வெகுளாமை, 'not becoming angry') recalls Chapter 31 (Vegulaamai), here applied to the one who is refused. The second line is read in more than one way: nirappidumbai thaaneyum saalum kari (நிரப்பிடும்பை தானேயும் சாலும் கரி) can mean that the asker's own poverty is sufficient witness (kari, கரி) that things are not always available when wanted (Puliyur Kesikan, Pappaiah), that the asker's poverty teaches him (Mu. Varadarasanar), or that the refuser may be in the same plight as himself (Kalaignar). The commentarial tradition following Parimelazhagar takes the beggar's own want as reason enough for patience toward a refusal. Pope: 'Askers refused from wrath must stand aloof; / The plague of poverty itself is ample proof.' The texts on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net agree.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Riches come now to one, now to another, and like the wheels of cars are ever rolling.”
hinduism.explanation: The Vedic hymn reminds the rich that wealth turns like a chariot wheel, moving from one person to another.
hinduism.tie_back: If fortune turns for everyone, the refused asker has no grounds for anger, since the giver too may be in want, which is Kalaignar's reading of the Kural.
hinduism.source: Rig Veda 10.117.5 (tr. Ralph T. H. Griffith)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com (second line of the verse); it addresses the rich, so the link to the asker's restraint is indirect.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Not that I speak in respect of want: for I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content.”
christianity.explanation: Thanking the Philippians for their gift, Paul says he has learned to be content whether he has plenty or is in want.
christianity.tie_back: Contentment in want is the inner freedom that lets an asker meet refusal without anger.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (bolls.life KJV text); good on the asker's inner state, though it does not mention refusal.

islam.quote_or_event: “Who spend [in the cause of Allāh] during ease and hardship and who restrain anger and who pardon the people - and Allāh loves the doers of good;”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an praises those who restrain anger and pardon people, together with those who give in ease and hardship.
islam.tie_back: Holding back anger and forgiving is what the Kural asks of the refused asker.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via the quran.com API; a general teaching on restraining anger, not specific to asking.

judaism.quote_or_event: Ben Zoma teaches that the rich person is the one who rejoices in his lot, and the mighty one is the one who conquers his own inclination.
judaism.explanation: Pirkei Avot locates wealth in contentment and strength in self-control.
judaism.tie_back: An asker who is content with his lot and masters his impulses will not rage at a refusal.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 4:1 (Mishnah Yomit, tr. Dr. Joshua Kulp, via Sefaria) (paraphrase)
judaism._accuracy_note: Next-best paraphrase, not re-verified verbatim this session; it concerns contentment and self-mastery generally, not refusal.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Happy indeed we live, we who possess nothing. Feeders on joy we shall be, like the Radiant Gods.”
buddhism.explanation: Tradition links this verse to the day the Buddha went for alms in a village and came back with an empty bowl, yet stayed joyful (cf. SN 4.18).
buddhism.tie_back: The Buddha's calm in front of an empty bowl is the mendicant's freedom from anger at refusal that the Kural asks for.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; the alms-round setting comes from the commentarial tradition and SN 4.18, which were not verified here.

jainism.quote_or_event: “He should beg food from the householder when his dinner is ready; a wise man should not care whether he gets alms or not. ‘I get nothing to-day, perhaps I shall get something to-morrow;’ a monk who thinks thus, will not be grieved by his want of success.”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira lists alabha, being refused, among the twenty-two hardships a monk must bear calmly, without grief or resentment.
jainism.tie_back: This is the Kural's rule that the asker must not be angered by refusal, made into a monastic discipline.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com (two consecutive verses joined, verse marker '(30)' omitted); a near one-to-one match on bearing refusal without resentment.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “For a moment he doubted whether or no to fly at Melanthius and kill him with his staff, or fling him to the ground and beat his brains out; he resolved, however, to endure it and keep himself in check”
greek_mythology.explanation: Kicked by the goatherd Melanthius while disguised as a beggar, Odysseus masters his anger and stays on the path.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The beggar who keeps himself in check is the Kural's asker who does not give way to anger.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on classics.mit.edu; good on a beggar's restraint, though he is provoked by abuse rather than by a simple refusal.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “He once begged alms of a statue, and, when asked why he did so, replied, ‘To get practice in being refused.’”
philosophy.explanation: Diogenes trained himself to meet refusal calmly by begging from a statue that could never give.
philosophy.tie_back: Practising refusal until it no longer stings is the Kural's advice that the asker must not be angered.
philosophy.source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of the Eminent Philosophers 6.49 (tr. R. D. Hicks)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Wikisource (inner quotation marks normalised); a near one-to-one match on accepting refusal.
